summary: If a deer grew five times bigger in every direction, it would weigh 125 times more but its leg bones would get only 25 times thicker. This paper shows how that one rule of size shapes lungs, guts, legs, eating habits and even bird flight.

blocks.kicker: Science desk / A picture story in four parts
blocks.title: Why size changes everything

chapters.title: Why not just make everything bigger?
chapters.caption: Say a deer grew five times bigger in every direction: five times taller, longer and wider. Is it five times stronger? Not quite. Its weight grows 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 times, but the slice across its leg bones grows only 5 × 5 = 25 times. Each bit of bone now carries five times more load.

media.alt: A small deer and a deer five times bigger stand side by side. The big one is not five times stronger, only five times taller.

chapters.title: Chop a cube
chapters.caption: Cut one big cube into 125 little cubes. You still have the same amount of stuff, but now there are lots of new faces. The outside grows 5 times bigger while the inside stays the same. So the smaller something is, the more outside it has for its inside.

media.alt: A big cube is chopped into 125 little cubes, and every little cube has its own outside.

chapters.title: Fold it, coil it, thicken it
chapters.caption: A tiny rotifer breathes through its skin. Make it twice as wide and its body needs 8 times more air, but its skin grows only 4 times. So bigger animals add outside: lungs and gills with many folds, and long guts with folded walls. Their legs get thicker too, like an elephant’s.

media.alt: Three fixes bodies use: thick legs, folded lungs and a long folded gut.

chapters.title: Birds follow the rule
chapters.caption: Flying has a size rule too. Weight per wing area is called wing loading. The authors lined up 14 real bird species from a data table: the more weight per wing, the faster the bird cruises. A kittiwake (0.41 kg) and a dove prion (0.20 kg) have almost the same wing loading, and almost the same speed: 10.1 and 9.9 metres per second.

media.alt: A chart of 14 bird species: birds with more weight per wing area cruise faster, along a straight line.

strips.title: The deer that got too big

panels.caption: Grow a deer 5 times bigger in every direction: taller, longer and wider.

media.alt: A small deer and a deer five times bigger in every direction.

panels.caption: Its weight is 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 times more. The slice across its leg bone is only 5 × 5 = 25 times bigger.

media.alt: Weight grows like a cube of blocks, 125 of them. The leg bone slice grows like a flat square, only 25 of them.

panels.caption: Each bit of bone now holds 5 times more weight. Crack! Big animals need thicker legs, like elephants.

media.alt: The big deer’s thin legs buckle and crack under its weight.

panels.caption: A tiny rotifer breathes straight through its skin. For its size, that is enough air.

media.alt: A tiny rotifer breathes air straight through its skin; little oxygen dots drift in.

panels.caption: Make it twice as wide: its body needs 8 times more air, but its skin is only 4 times bigger.

media.alt: If a rotifer were twice as wide, its body would need 8 times more air but its skin would grow only 4 times.

panels.caption: So bigger animals grow folded surfaces: branching lungs, comb-like gills and a long, folded gut.

media.alt: Big animals grow folded surfaces: branching lungs, comb-like gills and a coiled, folded gut.

strips.title: Why tiny animals snack all day

panels.caption: A warm body loses heat through its outside. A mouse has lots of outside for its size. An elephant has much less.

media.alt: A mouse with many heat waves rising off it, next to an elephant with only a few.

panels.caption: So small animals, like mice and hummingbirds, need rich, high-calorie food again and again, such as nuts and sugary nectar.

media.alt: The mouse nibbles seeds and a hummingbird sips sugary nectar: small animals eat rich food again and again.

panels.caption: Big animals lose less heat for their size, so an elephant can live on leaves, and a huge blue whale on tiny krill.

media.alt: An elephant eats low-calorie leaves while a huge blue whale eats tiny krill: big bodies lose less heat for their size.
